paras: The Walterboro jail lynching threat was an August 1895 episode in South Carolina in which a mob from Hampton county was reported preparing to lynch six Black prisoners held in the Colleton county jail at Walterboro. Deputies spirited the men out of town through the swamps and by boat and train to the state penitentiary in Columbia, and no one was harmed. South Carolina and Savannah papers told the story as a narrow escape, under headlines such as "Defeated Lynchers" and "Ropes for Six."

Five of the prisoners, William Blake, William Frazer, Cato Graves, Prince Graves and William Dix, were charged with the murder of a white man named Meares, who was killed in his barn yard in Hampton county. The State reported that three of them had confessed, and the Columbia Register said Meares had been killed "for the purpose of robbery." According to the Register, the killing "caused intense excitement," and the prisoners were taken to the Walterboro jail for safety.
Held with them was W. C. Mimms, accused of killing a Capt. Mixson about a year earlier, whose conviction had been set aside for a new trial that was later postponed after his lawyer died.

On Thursday, August 22, a rumor spread in Walterboro that a mob would come that night to lynch the prisoners, and later in the afternoon a number of men arrived whom the Register called the mob's advance guard. Sheriff Black of Colleton county had his son, Deputy Sheriff John Black, swear in five special deputies and take the prisoners to the penitentiary. In the deputy's own account, four Hampton men saw the party leave town about five o'clock and were thought to have alerted others waiting for nightfall to attack the jail.

The Register wrote that the crowd in town caught on and gave chase, while the guarded party crossed the swamp, reached the Ashepoo River and rowed several miles downstream with the prisoners at the oars. At the Ashepoo trestle the deputies flagged down the Charleston and Savannah fast mail with the bridge keeper's lantern and rode to Charleston. From there they reached Columbia by way of Sumter, avoiding a rail line where they feared interception.

By Governor Evans's orders the six were lodged in the state penitentiary, where The State said they would stay until their trial and then be returned to Hampton county. No arrest of any would-be lyncher, and no report of the Meares trial, appears in the coverage.

The story ran only in the white press, starting with a Columbia dispatch in the Savannah Morning News on August 25 that relayed Deputy Black's account under the headline "Defeated Lynchers." The State's report, naming the deputies and prisoners, appeared in the Morning News's South Carolina column on August 26 and in Sumter's Watchman and Southron as "Escape Lynching" on August 28. The Charleston Southern Christian Advocate's weekly summary listed it more cautiously as a "rumored" lynching party foiled by removing "the murderers of R. Mears."

The Columbia Register's version, reprinted in the Manning Times as "Ropes for Six," was the fullest and the most mocking. It described a mob "bent on stringing the whole outfit to so many trees," and closed by calling the prisoners "the happiest negroes in South Carolina." None of the white reports questioned the prisoners' guilt, and the Advocate's summary called them murderers outright. No Black-press report of the episode was found.

The reports differ on details: The State gave the fifth defendant as William Dix, Sr. and the Register as William Dix, Jr., and they placed the Meares killing "about a week ago" and "several weeks ago." The State's text put the arrival in Columbia on Saturday, while the Register and the Charleston summary placed it on Friday, August 23.

reader.title: Walterboro jail lynching threat (1895)
bases: A mob from Hampton county was reported preparing to lynch six Black prisoners in the Colleton county jail, who were spirited away by deputies before any attack (A1, A3, A4).

No one was killed: the prisoners were removed to the state penitentiary before the reported mob reached them (A1, A3, A4). The episode was a threatened lynching over a murder accusation, carried out by a mob of unstated size (A3).

The Morning News's Columbia dispatch (A1), the Columbia Register (A3) and The State (A2, A4) independently report the threatened mob and the removal, though a Charleston weekly summary calls the lynching party only 'rumored' (A5).

accounts.label: Deputy Sheriff Black (Columbia dispatch)
accounts.gist: The party left Walterboro about 5 p.m. after word that a Hampton mob was coming; four Hampton men saw them leave, and a 'race' through swamps and across a river foiled pursuit before the deputies flagged the fast mail at the Ashepoo trestle.

accounts.label: Columbia Register
accounts.gist: A mob was rumored Thursday; men arrived in the afternoon as an advance guard; the deputies took the prisoners out at night, the town crowd pursued, and the party escaped by rowing down the Ashepoo to the railroad bridge.

accounts.label: The State
accounts.gist: Sheriff Black heard a mob was coming from Hampton county that night and had his son swear in deputies and take the prisoners under guard through swamps to the Ashepoo trestle and on to Columbia.

accounts.label: Charleston weekly summary
accounts.gist: Lists as 'rumored' that a lynching party formed in Hampton county and was foiled by removing the prisoners.

framing.detail: The Columbia Register's 'Ropes for Six' joked about 'six happy negroes' and stringing them 'to so many trees', while treating the sheriff's removal as proper and the mob as 'infuriated'.
The Savannah Morning News headed its dispatch 'Defeated Lynchers' and called the deputy's story 'a wierd one'; The State's item ran as 'Escape Lynching' in Sumter.
